report_name: Chaos Ransomware Uses Browser-Based 'msaRAT' to Evade Detection

threat_actors.name: Chaos
threat_actors.description: A ransomware group deploying the msaRAT to establish a stealthy foothold in victim networks and evade detection by routing C2 traffic through legitimate web browsers.

attack_patterns.name: Phishing
attack_patterns.description: The infection chain for msaRAT typically starts with vishing or spam emails containing a malicious MSI installer disguised as a Windows update.

attack_patterns.name: Remote Access Software
attack_patterns.description: msaRAT is a remote access trojan that abuses legitimate browser software (Chrome, Edge) to establish a command and control channel, effectively using the browser as a remote access tool.

attack_patterns.name: Application Layer Protocol
attack_patterns.description: msaRAT uses the WebRTC protocol, a standard web protocol, to establish its command and control data channel, making the traffic appear as legitimate browser activity.

attack_patterns.name: Proxy
attack_patterns.description: The C2 signaling process is obscured using legitimate cloud services as proxies, including Cloudflare Workers and a Twilio TURN relay server, to hide the true IP address of the attacker's C2 server.

attack_patterns.name: Encrypted Channel
attack_patterns.description: msaRAT uses a layered encryption approach for its C2 communications. The entire channel is wrapped in the standard DTLS encryption used by WebRTC, and an inner layer of ChaCha-Poly1305 encryption is used for the actual commands and data.

malware.name: msaRAT
malware.description: A Rust-based remote access trojan (RAT) that evades network detection by launching a headless instance of Chrome or Edge and routing its C2 communications through a WebRTC data channel established via the Chrome DevTools Protocol.

tools.name: Google Chrome
tools.description: Abused by msaRAT, which launches a headless instance of the browser to establish a WebRTC data channel for command and control.

tools.name: Microsoft Edge
tools.description: Abused by msaRAT, which launches a headless instance of the browser to establish a WebRTC data channel for command and control.

tools.name: Cloudflare Workers
tools.description: Used by msaRAT for initial C2 signaling, acting as a proxy to hide the true C2 infrastructure.

tools.name: Twilio
tools.description: A Twilio TURN relay server is used by msaRAT to further obscure C2 communications and prevent a direct peer-to-peer connection.

infrastructure.name: msaRAT C2 Infrastructure
infrastructure.description: C2 infrastructure for msaRAT that uses Cloudflare Workers for initial signaling and a Twilio TURN relay server to proxy communications and hide the true C2 server location.

indicators.name: Suspicious Headless Browser With Remote Debugging Port
indicators.pattern:
title: Suspicious Headless Browser With Remote Debugging Port
id: 2b8a1c9d-5e6f-4a7b-8c9d-0e1f2a3b4c5d
status: experimental
description: Detects Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge being launched in headless mode with the remote debugging port enabled. This is a TTP used by the msaRAT malware to evade network detection by routing C2 traffic through the browser.
references:
  - https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/
author: cyber.netsecops.io
date: 2026-07-23
tags:
  - attack.t1219
  - attack.command_and_control
level: high
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\msedge.exe'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - '--headless'
      - '--remote-debugging-port='
  condition: selection
indicators.description: Detects the execution of a web browser in headless mode with the remote debugging port enabled, a technique used by msaRAT to create a covert C2 channel.
